content: The second edition of the Guideline on Infant Feeding in Areas of Zika Virus Transmission was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2021. This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for infant feeding practices in regions where Zika virus transmission is ongoing. It is available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-002918-7 and 978-92-4-002919-4. Under the terms of the WHO license, the content of this guideline can be copied, redistributed, and adapted for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation of the guideline is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that WHO is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The guideline addresses critical questions regarding breastfeeding and expressed breast milk in areas with Zika virus transmission. It evaluates whether breastfeeding by a lactating woman infected with Zika virus increases the risk of transmitting the virus to the infant. It also explores modifications to infant feeding practices for infants affected by complications associated with Zika virus, such as congenital Zika syndrome or Guillain-Barré syndrome, and the support required for caregivers of these infants. The guideline emphasizes the importance of exclusive breastfeeding for infants aged 0–6 months and continued breastfeeding up to 2 years and beyond. It highlights that the benefits of breastfeeding outweigh any potential risks of Zika virus transmission through breast milk. Although Zika virus has been detected in breast milk, there is no conclusive evidence that it can cause infection in infants. Other bodily fluids exchanged during breastfeeding, such as sweat and blood, are also considered in the context of potential transmission. Zika virus infection during pregnancy can lead to severe complications, including microcephaly and other congenital anomalies collectively known as congenital Zika syndrome. It is also associated with preterm birth, miscarriage, and nervous system complications such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, neuropathy, and myelitis. Infants with congenital Zika syndrome may experience feeding difficulties, including dysphagia, gastroesophageal reflux, and delayed gastric emptying, which can negatively impact their nutritional status and growth. The guideline provides recommendations for feeding modifications tailored to the severity of the infant's condition, such as postural adjustments, environmental modifications, and thickening of feeds. It also underscores the importance of supporting caregivers to improve the growth, nutritional status, developmental milestones, and quality of life of affected infants. The development of this guideline followed rigorous procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. It incorporates direct and indirect evidence, systematic reviews, and expert input. WHO acknowledges the contributions of numerous individuals and organizations, including members of the Guideline Development Group, peer reviewers, and systematic review teams. Financial support for this work was provided by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and the United States Agency for International Development, with no influence on the content or recommendations. The primary audience for this guideline includes health professionals responsible for developing national and local health protocols, particularly those related to infant feeding. It is also intended for healthcare providers, such as nurses, general practitioners, pediatricians, and program managers, as well as pregnant or breastfeeding women living in or traveling to areas with Zika virus transmission. The guideline aims to assist WHO Member States and their partners in making informed decisions to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, improve maternal and child nutrition, and address the challenges posed by Zika virus transmission. It is part of WHO's broader efforts to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding as a critical component of quality healthcare and emergency response.
